role: trained LLM serving as an evaluator-judge for the LitBench creative-writing preference dataset, writing a paragraph-length rationale explaining why one r/WritingPrompts story is preferred over another in a head-to-head matchup (the rationale walks through Story A, then Story B, then a comparative verdict citing concrete craft elements)
input_unit: head-to-head rationale (a multi-paragraph LLM-authored judgment that names craft strengths and weaknesses of two competing stories written to the same WritingPrompts prompt, ending with a verdict for the CHOSEN STORY)
target: two competing short-fiction responses to a single r/WritingPrompts prompt — Story A and Story B — one of which is designated CHOSEN STORY at the top of the input
inline_evidence_example: the phrase "the prose suffers from repetition, awkward phrasing, and some grammatical errors" is a complaint that evidences a 'sentence-level polish / line-edit cleanliness' norm without naming it; the phrase "the transition from the brink of death to a mystical, otherworldly forest is handled smoothly, and the imagery of the green light blooming into a new forest is evocative" is praise that evidences a 'scene transition smoothness' norm AND a 'concrete sensory imagery' norm; the phrase "the story lingers on the domestic scene and magical mechanics but loses tension when it tries to introduce external stakes" is a complaint that evidences a 'pacing / tension management across a scene' norm; the phrase "the twist—where the boy betrays two of the witches to the soldiers—adds surprise and emotional resonance" is praise that evidences a 'twist effectiveness' norm AND an 'emotional payoff' norm; the phrase "ends with a somewhat anticlimactic decision to investigate, without a strong dramatic payoff" is a complaint that evidences an 'ending impact / dramatic payoff' norm
polarity_hint: Every LitBench rationale is a STRUCTURED HEAD-TO-HEAD: it discusses Story A (a paragraph), then Story B (a paragraph), then closes with an explicit comparative verdict siding with the CHOSEN STORY named at the top. Both the WINNER (chosen) and LOSER (not chosen) are routinely mixed-polarity — the rationale almost always concedes some craft strength of the loser and notes some limitation of the winner — so MIXED-polarity passages are common. When extracting signals, the polarity of an individual signal must reflect the EVALUATIVE STANCE of that signal alone (praise of the loser = positive, complaint about the winner = negative), independent of which story finally wins. Norms cited typically span: PROSE-LEVEL craft (sentence-level polish, grammatical correctness, repetition/redundancy, awkward phrasing, prose register, imagery vividness, sensory detail, line-edit cleanliness); VOICE (distinctness, consistency, register fit, narrator credibility); CHARACTER (agency, depth, motivation clarity, sympathetic vs unsympathetic protagonist, character arc); PLOT/STRUCTURE (narrative arc completeness, pacing balance between scene and summary, scene-to-scene momentum, plot focus vs digression, world-building integration, exposition load); DIALOGUE (sharpness, economy, character-revealing function, tag punctuation, naturalness); OPENING/HOOK (in-medias-res vs scene-setting, immediate stakes, first-line strength); ENDING (twist effectiveness, payoff strength, satisfying-vs-abrupt resolution, thematic landing, anticlimax); STAKES (stakes establishment, emotional resonance, reader engagement, immersion); TONE (consistency, tonal blending humor/horror, tonal wavering as a flaw); PROMPT FIDELITY (how well the story executes on the WritingPrompts premise, originality of the take, subverting expectations); LENGTH ECONOMY (concise/punchy vs sprawling/meandering, overwritten passages, ambition-vs-execution tradeoffs, unfocused storytelling, gratuitous content). The rationale also frequently invokes META-evaluative criteria like "the average reader is likely to prefer X" — these comparative-verdict sentences are themselves signal-rich (extract them as observation/praise/complaint with rubric_matches=[]). Bare verdicts with no craft reasoning ("A is better") are not signals on their own — but they are almost never present in this corpus; rationales always cite reasons.
